In reasoning model development, it's always been this interesting tension between training/optimizing chain-of-thoughts (CoTs) vs not touching them to preserve monitorability. CoTs are cool because we can check what the model is up to (e.g., whether it cheats or not) as long as it spells out its thought process. And we risk losing that if we explicitly optimize CoTs. Two caveats: 1) I.e., the catch of CoT and monitorability is that this only works if the written thinking reflects what the model is actually doing. 2) Also, when models become more capable, they spell out less in the CoT (like a cleverer math student needs less note-taking when solving problems during an exam). Nothing new on that front, but an interesting thread below on how to measure "harder to monitor", with some interesting results that confirm the existing intuitions: 1) no-CoT capability (meaning how much reasoning the model can do in a single forward pass without writing anything down) - Better pretraining (lower perplexity) raises this no-CoT capability - Architecture mostly doesn't matter 2) CoT controllability (meaning how well the model can change its written reasoning when asked to add, remove, or change parts of it) - RL alone raises controllability a lot - Controllability is passed on through distillation * Higher no-CoT capability and higher controllability both make monitoring harder. PS: Perhaps the good news is that it seems that process supervision wasn't the main culprit. (1/10) Today, we’re sharing new research from @OpenAI: How does CoT monitorability (no-CoT capability and CoT controllability) evolve over the model training lifecycle? We emerged with unsurprising but sobering findings: as we scale toward more intelligent systems, models are be…

Super interesting work on agent memory. (this is a must-read) It discusses whether agents can manage their own memory. If so, what would that self-organized memory look like? This is the closest implementation that I have seen to my own memory system. I mostly use linked documents with my agents, and it has been working extremely well. It works well because frontier models have gotten better at persisting external knowledge. The problem: Memory systems usually fix the schema in advance, with set record types and rules for how to group them. The solution: SoMem gives the agent ordinary linked documents instead. The agent decides what to summarize, which topics to create, and when to revise them. Every summary links back to the original interaction as evidence, and the runtime builds time, relation, and recency views on top. At question time, the agent chooses what to search and follows links to the source when it needs to check. SoMem beat the strongest baseline by 2.66 points on LoCoMo, 3.10 on BEAM-100K, and 2.00 on LongMemEval-S. Memory built by one model also worked when read by another. If your agent already reads and writes files, try letting it organize memory as linked notes before adding a vector store. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.11929 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/can-llm-agents-organize-their-own-memory-2611.11929

Recursive self-improvement is one of the most discussed ideas in AI right now. Banger paper on RSI for frontier pre-training. They claim to be the first in the world to apply RSI to an entire frontier pre-training run from scratch. This work uses agent-driven loops on a single frontier pre-training run and produced 801-30B-A3B, an open 30B MoE base that beats Qwen3-30B-A3B and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B. Pre-training is hard to improve with one big loop. A run costs hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours and happens once, and its real goal is headroom for post-training. So they split the work into smaller loops that can close. Agents debug infrastructure and data, check post-training headroom with tiny SFT runs, and turn expert judgment into metrics for data pipelines. A shared context store keeps negative results across teams. With only 6B tokens of SFT and no RL, the model had the highest average on four agentic benchmarks against fully post-trained models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10719 Chat with Paper: https://academy.dair.ai/papers/no-second-run-does-rsi-stop-at-frontier-pre-training-2611.10719

Five minutes after I gave lemlist 30 companies to pitch for sponsorships, the campaign was loaded. I still had to read it before putting my name on it. I used to block a full morning to build these lists. I sell newsletter placements and LinkedIn/X posts to ecommerce and B2B SaaS brands, prospecting to fill gaps in my calendar. I typed this in Claude through lemlist's MCP; @lemlist found contacts, verified emails and built the sequence: "Find the person who runs partnerships and the most senior marketing leader at these 30 companies. Verify every email. Tell me which companies have neither role so I can drop them, then build a 4-step email sequence for the rest and show me the preview. Don't send anything." → 16 companies had neither role in lemlist's database, so I dropped them → 23 people across 14 companies → 22 of 23 emails found and run through verification Reading every row, I found three contacts with wrong-company domains or outdated jobs, plus one missing email. Removing those contacts cut three companies; I deliberately kept one contact per company, leaving 11. Nothing reaches a real inbox unread. I saved the four-step sequence as a draft, then kept this run small by sending only the first email to those 11 people, with follow-ups skipped. All 11 were delivered, and one person has replied positively. This is the lemlist MCP I used: https://www.lemlist.com/product/lemlist-mcp?utm_source=x&utm_campaign=influ_chasedimond&utm_content=post1 P.S. What takes you longer when building a prospect list: finding the right person or checking their details?
The mission has not and will not change
